103:1: Allah swears by time. The word has been interpreted as the afternoon in particular and as time as a whole. [The Arabic word العصر, al-ʿaṣr, also invites reflection through the related sense of pressing or squeezing something to draw out what it contains; this is a linguistic image, distinct from the interpretations of the oath.] These reflections converge on one truth: time is running out. The end of the day is like the final minutes of a long examination, when there is no room for play. The image of melting capital recalls the story told of an ice seller calling attention to his stock as it melted away. Your life is not money stored safely away: every breath that leaves you is gone for good. Wasting health and free time is therefore a grievous loss, not a minor setback. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “There are two blessings in which many people incur loss: health and free time.” (Sahih al-Bukhari, 6412).

Reflecting on time changes how you see the day. [The Arabic image associated with العصر returns here: either you press your time for the obedience and useful work it can yield, or time presses you onward toward the end of your life.] No part of the day is without consequence. Understanding that an end is approaching makes you more attentive to how things end: the close of a day or a lifetime calls for greater effort, not neglect of Allah. A believer moves from one useful task to another, doing even worldly work well and seeking Allah’s pleasure through it. They do not let free time become a vast space that consumes their life unnoticed.
103:2: The oath is followed by a frightening conclusion: “man is in utter loss”. [In Arabic, إِنَّ and the emphatic لَـ reinforce this statement; فِي means ‘in’.] The verse does not say that people lose out only occasionally. It places them within loss, as though loss surrounds them on every side: time consumes their capital, worldly life makes what wastes it seem attractive, and other people may draw them into their own standards. Al-Asr’s position between At-Takathur and Al-Humazah highlights two ways this happens: becoming preoccupied with others through rivalry, or through mockery and fault-finding. Alongside these comes accumulating and counting wealth, until its owner imagines that it will prolong their life.

A person may begin by wanting to have more than others, then look down on them once they feel superior. Their life slips away in comparison, envy, ridicule and accumulation that never satisfies. Loss does not arise only from committing major forbidden acts; it can also come from selling your most precious resources—health and time—for something trivial. Every moment therefore asks a question: what am I obtaining in exchange for my life? What surrounds me and draws me toward loss? Your surroundings may themselves be part of the problem. Those closest to you can help you prepare for the Hereafter or distract you from it. Regretting time after it has gone is not enough. You need a pattern of life that makes time for prayer, remembrance of Allah, learning, work, family ties and serving others, and that measures worth by the Hereafter rather than people’s admiration.
103:3: The exception reveals the way to salvation: “except those who believe”. [The Arabic expression إِلَّا الَّذِينَ, ‘except those who’, is plural.] This suggests a community whose members strengthen one another, rather than an isolated individual’s undertaking. Faith is the first foundation. It is more than information: it gives a new perspective in which attending a funeral becomes an opportunity for reward, illness an occasion for worship, prayer a central appointment, and time capital for the Hereafter. Then come the words “and do righteous deeds”. [The Arabic الصَّالِحَاتِ is plural: righteous deeds.] Faith awakens a person to improve what they can. They do not settle comfortably for one good deed while neglecting other avenues of goodness. Nor do they close themselves off from others: “and exhort one another to the truth”.

Preoccupation with other people brought loss in At-Takathur and Al-Humazah. Here, concern for them becomes a means of salvation when it takes the form of sincere advice, mercy and helping them escape harm. This counsel is mutual: today you advise your brother, and tomorrow he advises you. No one is too important to receive advice or too insignificant to offer it. Good companionship is therefore essential. Someone living among people who pull every person seeking purification back into their habits resembles someone washing in a place that soils them again each time. Finally come the words “and exhort one another to patience”. Many set out, but few reach the end. It is easy to become enthusiastic about a decision to obey Allah; sustaining it for months and years is harder.

Patience keeps faith, good deeds and calling people to Allah from being abandoned. Encouraging one another to persevere helps prevent each person from falling alone: when one weakens, another supports them. In three verses, the surah presents a complete way to salvation: valuing time, faith that transforms how we see, deeds that fill a lifetime, a community that counsels one another in truth, and patience that carries them to the finish.
